sources.title: All hail electrification. But let’s talk about the hard part.

items.title: The IEA's Head Says Energy's Three Objectives Are Getting Aligned
items.body: Fatih Birol, who heads the International Energy Agency, discussed concepts from the agency's report at the United Nations the following day. He described an energy world defined by choices and trade-offs, then argued the terms have changed: when he looks at the world today, for the first time in years, all of these three objectives are getting aligned. The claim is not that one objective has won, but that the three have stopped pulling apart.

items.title: A Misconduct Accusation Is Turning Arizona Voters Away From a Republican, NPR Reports
items.body: NPR reports that Mark Lamb, a Republican candidate for Congress in Arizona, has been accused of sexual misconduct while he was sheriff. In the same report, the controversy is described as turning many voters away, and Democrats are said to see an opportunity in the red seat.

sources.title: Paul Rudd Says He Stopped Bringing His Phone to Film Sets Because He’s ‘Addicted Like Everybody Else’: ‘They’re Facilitating Our Own Destruction’

discussion.body: Twelve jurors work because you can track every face and know what each one wants. Twenty experts is a crowd, and the risk is a lecture with a moderator and a lot of nodding.

The crowd might be the point. A climate deliberation where no single expert can settle the question is precisely the frustration the format can dramatize, and twenty is a fair stand-in for a problem nobody can adjudicate alone.

items.title: Twenty Experts in One Room: The Jury-Room Engine Behind 'A Statement'
items.body:
Paul Rudd plays the moderator of the first-ever meeting dedicated to solving America's climate crisis in "A Statement," and Variety's description of the film is mostly a description of a room: a Florida beachside resort in 1980, twenty experts, a weekend in a conference room, a setup the paper likens to "12 Angry Men."

The jury-room template is one of the most dependable engines in film, and the reason is arithmetic as much as writing. A fixed cast in a fixed space has nowhere to escape to, so every turn has to be somebody in that room changing position. Move the headcount from a jury to twenty experts and the pressure changes in two directions at once: more positions get represented, which is exactly what a climate deliberation seems to need, and more faces compete for attention, which is exactly what a film has to solve. Rudd's moderator is the role the format demands — with twenty people in the room, someone has to hold the floor.

Set the thing in 1980 and the audience arrives carrying decades of hindsight the characters cannot have. Whether the film plays that gap as irony or as tragedy is the bet worth watching.

sources.title: Australia investigating Flydubai co-pilot's links to country

items.title: Australia Investigates a Flydubai Co-Pilot Who Tried to Take the Controls
items.body:
The BBC reports that state police and Australia's security agency are looking into a Flydubai co-pilot who attempted to take control of a plane travelling to Israel. The inquiry concerns the man's links to the country.

Cockpit crew are the people the rest of aviation security is designed to trust. An alleged attempt from inside the flight deck — before any question of luggage, lists or screening — is the kind of case that makes the trust itself the thing being audited.

sources.title: Bosnia-Herzegovina votes amid divisive campaigns, EU bid

items.title: Bosnia and Herzegovina Votes for Parliament, a Presidency and Local Councils
items.body: Polls have opened in Bosnia and Herzegovina, DW reports, with voters taking part in parliamentary, presidential and local elections. Voters are filling three levels of government at once — national and subnational contests decided by the same people on the same day, each of which can turn on a completely different argument.

sources.title: Voting in Brazil's 2026 presidential election has begun, with polls showing Lula and Bolsonaro nearly tied

items.title: Brazil's presidential runoff is likely, but the names on the ballot are the story
items.body:
Voting has begun in Brazil's 2026 presidential election. DW reports that Flavio Bolsonaro, son of former far-right president Jair Bolsonaro, is taking on incumbent left-wing president Lula da Silva, and that polls show the first round will likely require a runoff.

That a Bolsonaro is on the ballot — the son rather than the former president — is the structural fact worth holding onto. The runoff language matters too: "likely" is the polling expectation, not a result, and a first round that produces no outright winner is a different contest than the one polls were measuring a week earlier.

sources.title: Ontario-based air ambulance carrying 6 missing off U.S. coast

items.title: A Gulfstream air ambulance and six people are missing off the US coast
items.body:
An Ontario-based air ambulance with six people aboard is missing off the US coast. Global News Canada reports that the Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement that it issued a Search and Rescue Alert for a Gulfstream G-100 at around 1:20 a.m. Saturday.

The aircraft is described as an air ambulance, which means the people on board were already in transit for medical reasons. The alert is a search notice, not an outcome.

sources.title: Jeremy Strong Defends Method Acting, Says He Doesn’t Feel the Need to ‘Apologize’ to Co-Stars Who May Think ‘I’m Taking It Too Seriously’

discussion.body: The interesting part isn't the method acting — plenty of actors do versions of it. It's that he's pre-declining to apologize rather than saying he's sorry after the fact. That's a claim about what collaboration entitles a co-star to, not a claim about how he prepares.
It could be less a philosophy than a reputation he's been handed. "Infamous" is doing work in that sentence; once a method is your brand, defending it becomes part of the job.

items.title: Jeremy Strong's defense of method acting rests on an unusual premise: that he owes no apology
items.body:
Jeremy Strong, whose commitment to method acting is now the thing he is most identified with, said on The New Yorker Radio Hour podcast that he doesn't feel the "need to apologize" to collaborators who may think he takes the process "too seriously."

Most actor talk about craft emphasizes service to the work or to the ensemble. Strong's framing is different in kind: the friction is treated as a fact to be disclosed rather than a cost to be minimized. Whether that reads as integrity or as an excuse is a judgment about the work, and the disagreement is more interesting than the verdict. He arrived at the debate mid-career, having also taken on the role of a tech billionaire on screen.

sources.title: Kyiv bridge hit in further Russian drone attack as German chancellor makes surprise visit

items.title: A Drone Hits a Kyiv Bridge With Traffic On It
items.body: Video shows a drone striking the Pivnichyi — Northern — Bridge in Kyiv as vehicles move across it, the impact producing a large fireball. The footage catches the weapon and the traffic occupying the same span at the same instant.

sources.title: ‘Digger’ Star Tom Cruise Says He’s “So Proud Of What We Created” Despite Poor Open At Theaters

discussion.body: Thanking the people who signed on is the cheapest graceful move available to a star after a soft opening. It costs nothing and nobody can dispute the sincerity.
The comparison does less work than it looks. Lions for Lambs being the last Cruise film to open this low is a fact about the last two decades of his career, not about this movie's quality.
Agreed — 'may be the lowest since' is career arithmetic, not a verdict. Which is also why the Instagram post is the only thing in the story carrying a point of view.

items.title: Tom Cruise Says He's Honored by 'Digger' Even as It May Be His Weakest Opening Since 2007
items.body: Deadline reports that Digger may be the lowest opening for a Tom Cruise film since 2007's Lions for Lambs. Cruise's reply, in an Instagram post, was not a defense of the numbers: he said he was honored to have had the opportunity to create the film alongside the people who joined him on Alejandro G. Iñárritu's movie. It is the standard graceful exit for a star — praise the collaborators, skip the grosses — and it leaves the more interesting question untouched: what a Cruise-Iñárritu film was supposed to be in the first place.

sources.title: Brilliance Of The Who’s Leader Shines In ‘Pete Townshend: Behind Blue Eyes,’ Screening At Hamptons & Mill Valley

items.title: The British Invasion Had Three Leaders; Only One Is Still Hard to Explain
items.body: Deadline frames the British invasion of the mid-1960s as a multi-pronged attack, led above all by the Beatles, the Rolling Stones and the Who, whose seismic impact on American and world culture it treats as settled history. Look at the people in charge, though, and the three bands stop being symmetrical: of those leaders, Deadline says, the Who's songwriter, Pete Townshend, is perhaps the most mysterious. It is a neat way of pointing at a gap in how the era gets told — the bands are canon, the man who wrote one band's songs less so.

sources.title: ‘A Statement’ Review: Tom McCarthy’s Talky Climate Crisis Seriocomedy Is Light Entertainment That Hardly Rakes the Muck

discussion.body: Dating it to 1980 does half the work before anyone speaks. The audience arrives knowing the meeting didn't fix the problem, so futility is already in the room.
That's also the trap. When the outcome is common knowledge, the film has to earn interest from the people at the table rather than from whether the table succeeds.

items.title: A Climate Story Confined to One Futile 1980 Meeting
items.body: IndieWire's review from the New York Film Festival puts Tom McCarthy's new film in a single room. The Oscar-winning writer-director casts a plushly appointed ensemble as the environmental stewards and scholars who tried to solve the climate crisis, and the film's scope, on this account, is one long-winded, futile meeting in St. Petersburg, Florida, in 1980.

sources.title: She died covering war for Fox News. Her parents blame the network — and a star reporter

items.title: Two Fox News Journalists Died in Ukraine; Their Families Are Suing the Network
items.body: NPR reports that family members of two Fox News journalists killed while covering the war in Ukraine are suing the network. Their claim, as NPR describes it, is that the network put getting the story ahead of its people — an allegation made in a lawsuit, not an established finding.
